exa.snippet:
# 21 CFR 178.3610: α-Methylstyrene-vinyltoluene resins, hydrogenated

- Citation: 21 CFR 178.3610
- Jurisdiction: United States
- Legal force: In force
- Version: 1989-06-12

---

Also cited as: 21 C.F.R. § 178.3610; 21 CFR § 178.3610. Authority: 21 U.S.C. 321, 342, 348, 379e.

Hydrogenated α-methylstyrene-vinyltoluene copolymer resins having a molar ratio of 1 α-methylstyrene to 3 vinyltoluene may be safely used as components of polyolefin film intended for use in contact with food, subject to the following provisions:

(a) Hydrogenated α-methylstyrene-vinyltoluene copolymer resins have a drop-softening point of 125° to 165 °C and a maximum absorptivity of 0.17 liter per gram centimeter at 266 nanometers, as determined by methods titled “Determination of Softening Point (Drop Method)” and “Determination of Unsaturation of Resin 1977,” which are incorporated by reference. Copies are available from the Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition (HFS-200), Food and Drug Administration, 5001 Campus Dr., College Park, MD 20740, or available for inspection at the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). For information on the availability of this material at NARA, call 202-741-6030, or go to: http://www.archives.gov/federal_register/code_of_federal_regulations/ibr_locations.html.

(b) The polyolefin film is produced from olefin polymers complying with § 177.1520 of this chapter, and the average thickness of the film in the form in which it contacts food does not exceed 0.002 inch.

Source: [42 FR 14609, Mar. 15, 1977, as amended at 47 FR 11847, Mar. 19, 1982; 54 FR 24898, June 12, 1989]

§ 178.3610 α-Methylstyrene-vinyltoluene resins, hydrogenated.

Hydrogenated α-methylstyrene-vinyltoluene copolymer resins having a molar ratio of 1 α-methylstyrene to 3 vinyltoluene may be safely used as components of polyolefin film intended for use in contact with [food](https://www.law.cornell.edu/definitions/index.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=5f3b7ccf4b3f4f15bfde1fba6edad879&term_occur=999&term_src=Title:21:Chapter:I:Subchapter:B:Part:178:Subpart:D:178.3610), subject to the following provisions:

(a) Hydrogenated α-methylstyrene-vinyltoluene copolymer resins have a drop-softening point of 125° to 165 °C and a maximum absorptivity of 0.17 liter per gram centimeter at 266 nanometers, as determined by methods titled “Determination of Softening Point (Drop Method)” and “Determination of Unsaturation of Resin 1977,” which are incorporated by reference. Copies are available from the Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition (HFS-200), Food and Drug Administration, 5001 Campus Dr., College Park, MD 20740, or available for inspection at the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). For information on the availability of this material at NARA, call 202-741-6030, or go to: http://www.archives.gov/federal_register/code_of_federal_regulations/ibr_locations.html.

(b) The polyolefin film is produced from olefin polymers complying with [§ 177.1520](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/177.1520) of this chapter, and the average thickness of the film in the form in which it contacts food does not exceed 0.002 inch.

linkup.title: Polyolefin vs PVC Shrink Wrap: Which Is Food-Safe?
linkup.snippet:
## Quick Answer  
Polyolefin (often sold as POF) is the food-safe default: it’s made without chlorine or plasticizers and is widely sold as FDA-compliant for direct food contact. PVC shrink film is generally not considered food-safe for direct contact because it relies on plasticizer chemicals to stay flexible, and those plasticizers can migrate into food — especially fatty items like cheese and meat. If a product is going to touch food directly, reach for polyolefin and confirm the compliance claim in writing.
Polyolefin shrink film is typically a multi-layer blend of polyethylene and polypropylene. It doesn’t need plasticizers to stay flexible, and it contains no chlorine, so it doesn’t carry the same migration or combustion concerns as PVC.
When you’re sourcing polyolefin for food use, look for the supplier to explicitly state FDA food-contact compliance (commonly referenced against the FDA’s food-contact substance regulations for polyolefin resins) rather than just assuming it because the film is labeled “polyolefin.” Reputable shrink-film suppliers will state this clearly on the spec sheet or product listing — if they don’t, ask before you buy.  
Polyolefin also tends to be the better performer technically: it’s clearer, more puncture-resistant, and shrinks tighter around irregular shapes than PVC, which is part of why it has become the default for retail food bundling even where food safety isn’t the deciding factor.

Part 178 of Title 21 CFR outlines regulations for indirect food additives, specifically adjuvants, production aids, and sanitizers. ## 1. What a Multi-Layer EVOH Barrier Film Extrusion Line Is

### The product it makes

A multi-layer EVOH barrier film is a flexible packaging web built from several polymer layers that are melted and joined in one pass. One of those layers is ethylene vinyl alcohol, known as EVOH, which gives the web its extremely low oxygen transmission.

### The machine in one sentence

The line is a group of extruders that melt different resins at the same time and feed them into one die, where the melts are stacked into a single web. A blown film version inflates a bubble and cools it with an internal cooling system; a cast film version lays the melt onto a chill roll.
